# STKCraft API reference

*Generated by `cargo xtask api-docs` from STKCraft 0.1.88 — do not edit by hand.*

## About this reference

This page is generated from STKCraft's source: the command registry, the crate manifests and the module documentation. Editing it by hand is pointless — the next generation overwrites it. Edit the code, or the document that describes the design.

Every command is reachable by every transport. The menus, the shortcuts, the command line, the control channel, the Model Context Protocol server and the assistant all dispatch a command by its id, so the table below is not an integration guide for one client: it is the surface.

## Commands

A command is the unit of user-visible behaviour. Its id never changes once released; its parameters declare their kind, so a caller sends a number, text or degrees and the engine receives the typed value.

| Id | Label | Menu | Parameters |
|:---|---|---|:---|
| `access.compute` | Compute Access | Access | `step-seconds` (number): Search step. Shorter is more thorough and slower |
| `access.targets` | Compute Target Access | Access | `step-seconds` (number): Search step. Shorter is more thorough and slower |
| `planet.access` | Planet-Centred Access | Access | `body` (text, required): The body the station stands on and the orbit is about, by IAU name (e.g. Mars, Titan)<br>`radius-km` (number, required): Circular orbit radius from the body's centre, km<br>`inclination-deg` (degrees, required): Orbit inclination from the body's ICRF equator, degrees<br>`latitude-deg` (degrees, required): Station planetodetic latitude on that body, degrees<br>`longitude-deg` (degrees, required): Station longitude east of the body's prime meridian, degrees<br>`mask-deg` (degrees): Sensor horizon mask, degrees above the local horizon<br>`hours` (number): How long to search, hours<br>`step-seconds` (number): Search step: shorter is more thorough and slower |
| `satellite.add` | Add Satellite | Satellite | `name` (text, required): A display name; need not be unique<br>`line1` (text, required): The first line of the two-line element set<br>`line2` (text, required): The second line of the two-line element set |
| `satellite.remove` | Remove Satellite | Satellite | `id` (number, required): The numeric id of the satellite to remove |
| `scenario.rename` | Rename Scenario | Scenario | `name` (text, required): The new scenario name |
| `scenario.set-duration` | Set Timeline Duration | Scenario | `seconds` (number, required): How long the timeline runs, in seconds. Must be positive |
| `station.add` | Add Ground Station | Station | `name` (text, required): A display name; need not be unique<br>`latitude` (degrees, required): Geodetic latitude, positive north<br>`longitude` (degrees, required): Longitude, positive east<br>`minimum-elevation` (degrees, required): The horizon mask; nothing below it is visible |
| `station.remove` | Remove Ground Station | Station | `id` (number, required): The numeric id of the station to remove |
| `station.sensor` | Set Station Sensor | Station | `id` (number, required): The numeric id of the station<br>`half-angle` (degrees, required): Half-angle of the field-of-view cone about the boresight, in degrees. 180 is the whole upper hemisphere<br>`max-range-km` (number): Maximum slant range in kilometres; omit for unlimited<br>`azimuth` (degrees): Boresight azimuth, clockwise from north. Default 0<br>`elevation` (degrees): Boresight elevation above the horizon. Default 90 (zenith) |
| `target.add` | Add Target | Target | `name` (text, required): A display name; need not be unique<br>`points` (text, required): The target's corners as `lat,lon` pairs separated by semicolons, e.g. `40.4,-3.7` for a point or `0,0;0,1;1,1` for a triangle<br>`half-angle` (degrees): Half-angle of the sensor's field-of-view cone. Default 180<br>`minimum-elevation` (degrees): The observer's horizon mask. Default 0 |

## Crates

The workspace is layered: a crate may depend only on a strictly lower layer, so the analysis can run in a window, in a terminal and in a browser tab without knowing which it is in.

| Crate | Layer | What it is |
|:---|:---|---|
| `stkcraft-framework-core` | `L0` | Units, error types and foundational value types for STKCraft |
| `stkcraft-framework-i18n` | `L0` | Interface translations: the Craft catalog format, lookup with fallback, and plurals |
| `stkcraft-framework-storage` | `L1` | The record, the cache and the vector store: one crate owns persistence |
| `stkcraft-framework-time` | `L1` | Time scales, leap seconds and epoch arithmetic for STKCraft |
| `stkcraft-astro-body` | `L2` | Solar-system bodies: constants, IAU rotation models and ellipsoids for STKCraft |
| `stkcraft-astro-frames` | `L2` | Reference frames and coordinate transforms for STKCraft |
| `stkcraft-astro-sgp4` | `L2` | SGP4/SDP4 near-Earth and deep-space propagation for STKCraft |
| `stkcraft-astro-access` | `L3` | Access geometry for STKCraft: line of sight, sensors and windows |
| `stkcraft-astro-ephemeris` | `L3` | Planetary ephemerides for STKCraft: a NAIF SPK reader and the trait it fills |
| `stkcraft-agent-knowledge` | `L3` | The user's own documents, searched before the model answers |
| `stkcraft-framework-extensions` | `L3` | The extension package contract: manifests, ids and trust tiers |
| `stkcraft-astro-engine` | `L4` | Scenario, commands and analysis for STKCraft |
| `stkcraft-agent-mcp` | `L5` | The MCP server that turns STKCraft's commands into an agent's tools |
| `stkcraft-ui-viewport` | `L5` | The 3D viewport for STKCraft |
| `stkcraft-agent-runtime` | `L6` | The model agent: a model driving STKCraft's own tools and skills |
| `stkcraft-agent-control` | `L6` | The control channel: a local socket another program drives the engine through |

## stkcraft-framework-core

Foundational types shared by every `STKCraft` crate.

This crate is the bottom of the dependency graph (L0): units, error types and the small value types that the time, frame and propagation layers all agree on. It has no knowledge of orbits, scenarios or rendering.

Units are newtypes rather than bare `f64` so that a call site cannot silently pass degrees where radians are expected. Conversions are explicit and named.

## stkcraft-framework-i18n

Interface translations, in the format the Craft apps share.

An interface string is written in English in the code and translated by a catalog: a plain-text table of `context <TAB> English <TAB> translation` rows, one per line. **English is the key.** There is no English catalog and no symbol table to keep in step, so the source text a translator sees is exactly the text the interface shows, and a string that nothing translates simply appears in English.

It is the `ArtCraft` family's format, not this project's invention: `storytold/craft-i18n` holds the shared catalogs, arbitrates the rules CI enforces, and the other Craft apps read the same tables. A translation written here can be contributed there, and a rule that disagrees with the shared checker is a bug in this crate rather than a local preference. See `docs/standards.md` and `docs/guides/localization.md`.

The rules, in short:

- **Contexts.** Usually empty. A plain word (`menu`, `preview`) tells apart two meanings of the same English, and only `@plural`, `@id` and `@msg` mean something to the code.

- **Placeholders.** `{name}` in the source must appear in the translation, in any order, and a trailing `…` in one needs one in the other. A translation that drops a placeholder produces a sentence that cannot be filled in, which is worse than showing English.

- **Plurals.** An `@plural` row's source is `one|other`; its translation lists the locale's forms in CLDR order. [`translations::Translations::trn`] chooses the form.

- **Partial catalogs are fine.** A missing row is not an error anywhere in this crate.

No network, no filesystem, no `unsafe`, and no panics: catalogs are parsed from text a caller read, and every problem is reported with the line that caused it. The `DeepSeek` translation that fills catalogs lives in `xtask`, above the app, because a translation request is a network call and the kernel must not have one.

## stkcraft-framework-storage

Persistence: the record, the cache and the vector store.

Every stored thing belongs to one of three stores, and which one is decided by **the question a reader asks of the data** rather than by convenience (`docs/design/storage.md`):

| Question | Store | In this crate |
|---|---|---|
| "What was the scenario, and what exactly did it compute?" | relational | [`Store`] — SQLite, `STRICT`, versioned |
| "Give me this value again, it will not have changed" | key-value | [`Cache`] — one file per key, CRC per value |
| "Which vectors are near this one?" | vector | [`Vectors`] — brute-force cosine, candidates only |

No other crate opens a database, writes a key-value file or issues SQL. A crate that needs to remember something asks this one. That rule is what keeps a stray JSON file from appearing beside the executable, which is the failure the storage design exists to prevent.

A record that came from outside — a document, a kernel, a scenario document — carries its **SHA-256 digest**. A computation row carries the digest of the inputs it ran on. Without them a row says what happened but not what it happened to, and an analysis that cannot be reproduced is the thing this project refuses to ship.

## stkcraft-framework-time

Time scales and epoch arithmetic for `STKCraft`.

Spacecraft analysis cannot use a single clock: orbit integration runs on a uniform scale (TAI, TT or TDB), while user-facing times and ephemeris files are in UTC, which has leap seconds. Mixing the two silently is the classic way to get a timing error that only shows up as a bad conjunction warning.

This crate makes the scale part of the type ([`TimeScale`]) and keeps every conversion explicit. The constants and the 1972-onward leap-second table follow the IAU SOFA / ERFA reference implementation, whose values are themselves taken from the IERS Conventions.

Calendar formatting and civil-date parsing go through `chrono`, per the suite standard; this crate owns only the scale offsets and the leap table.

## stkcraft-astro-body

The bodies of the solar system, as the IAU describes them.

This crate answers three questions about a body and nothing else:

1. **How big and how massive is it?** [`Body::gm_km3_s2`] and [`Body::radii_km`], from DE440 and the IAU working group's cartographic constants.

2. **How is it oriented?** [`Body::orientation`] evaluates the IAU 2015 rotation model — pole right ascension and declination, and the prime meridian angle `W` — and [`Orientation::icrf_to_body_fixed`] turns that into the matrix that rotates ICRF vectors into the body-fixed frame.

3. **Where on its surface is a point?** [`Ellipsoid`], with planetocentric and planetodetic (planetographic) latitudes converted against the body's own ellipsoid rather than a hard coded WGS-84.

Constants and rotation models come from NAIF's `pck00011.tpc` and `gm_de440.tpc`, which are the machine-readable realisations of the IAU 2015 rotation model (Archinal et al. 2018, CMDA 130:22) and of the DE440 masses (Park et al. 2021, AJ 161:105). The tables in [`generated`] are generated from those files and every one of them carries the file and its checksum in the module comment.

The transformation convention is not assumed. It is pinned by tests against CSPICE (`pxform`) over the same kernel: the matrices this crate produces agree with CSPICE to 1e−11 for every body whose model is fully transcribed, and the one body that is not (Mars) has a test that records the known difference instead of hiding it. See `docs/plans/2026-11-05-solar-system-kernel.md`.

It does not know where a body *is* — that is the ephemeris crate's job — and it does not propagate anything. Positions and orientations are separate questions with separate sources, and keeping them apart is what lets each be verified against its own reference.

## stkcraft-astro-frames

Reference frames and coordinate transforms for `STKCraft`.

An orbit is meaningless without the frame it is expressed in, and turning a state vector into something a 3D view can draw means walking a chain of frame conversions: ICRF to GCRF, GCRF to the Earth-fixed frame through precession, nutation and Earth rotation, and then to the local horizon of a ground station.

This crate owns that chain. It built the frame identities and the fixed rotations first; the time-dependent rotations (precession, nutation, polar motion) arrive as separate, individually tested pieces.

## stkcraft-astro-sgp4

SGP4 and SDP4 propagation for `STKCraft`.

A two-line element set is a mean-element description of an Earth satellite paired with an empirical drag term. SGP4 turns it into an inertial state vector at any time within a few days of the element set's epoch; SDP4 is the same theory with the lunar and solar perturbations handled analytically for orbits whose period exceeds 225 minutes.

This crate is a from-scratch implementation of the published theory, written against the algorithm description and the reference implementation in:

- **Vallado, D. A., Crawford, P., Hujsak, R. and Kelso, T. S.**, *Revisiting Spacetrack Report 3*, AIAA 2006-6753, AIAA/AAS Astrodynamics Specialist Conference, Keystone, CO,

2006. Source code, test cases and expected output published by `CelesTrak` at <https://celestrak.org/publications/AIAA/2006-6753/>.

- **Hoots, F. R. and Roehrich, R. L.**, *Models for Propagation of NORAD Element Sets*, Spacetrack Report #3, Aerospace Defense Command, December 1980.

The 2006 paper exists because the 1980 report and the versions in circulation had diverged; its reference code is what the operational catalogues actually use, and its `tforverf.out` output is the verification reference this crate is tested against.

The test module runs all 33 of the paper's verification cases — near-Earth, half-day and one-day resonances, an 18-hour orbit, sub-orbital and decayed cases, and the deliberately broken element sets — and compares the position and velocity against the published output.

The two halves of the theory are held to different tolerances, because they are in different states, and the difference is stated rather than averaged away:

- **Near-Earth** results reproduce the published table to within `4e-9 km`, which is the limit of what a table printed to eight decimals can express.

- **Deep-space** results are currently within about 85 km worst case, and the resonant cases are the poor ones. The tolerance in the test is set to that measured accuracy, so a regression fails, but it is recorded as a known limitation in `CHANGELOG.md` rather than presented as a result.

- **TLE text is parsed strictly.** A malformed line is an error with the column named; nothing is guessed and nothing is silently defaulted.

- **Alpha-5** object identifiers are carried through as text, not decoded to a number.

- **No frame conversion.** Output is TEME, the frame SGP4 is defined in. Converting to ICRF or Earth-fixed belongs to `stkcraft-astro-frames`.

## stkcraft-astro-access

Access geometry for `STKCraft`: line of sight, sensors and visibility windows.

This is the layer that answers the question the product exists to answer: **when can this satellite see that ground station, and for how long.** Everything here is a pure function of positions and a time interval; nothing knows about orbits, files or windows.

Coverage analysis — a grid or a region evaluated over time — is a separate layer that is not built yet. This crate computes the visibility predicate and the windows, which is what a coverage grid will call; it does not compute percentages.

The pieces, in dependency order:

- [`ellipsoid`] — the WGS-84 Earth, so a station sits where it really is.

- [`site`] — a geodetic station and the local east/north/up axes at it.

- [`geometry`] — elevation, azimuth and range from a site to a target.

- [`sensor`] — the acceptance region around those angles.

- [`occultation`] — whether the Earth is in the way.

- [`window`] — turning a visibility predicate into start and end times.

The line of sight is the **geometric straight line**. There is no atmospheric refraction, no light-time correction and no aberration:

- **Refraction** is zero above about `5°` elevation and reaches half a degree at the horizon. It is not modelled, so a horizon mask at or near `0°` is a geometric horizon, not an optical one.

- **Light time** is at most `0.24 s` for a geostationary satellite, which moves the answer by a fraction of an arcsecond. Not modelled.

Both are real omissions and are named here so a result is not read as more precise than it is. Neither is approximated with a plausible-looking formula.

## stkcraft-astro-ephemeris

Where the planets are.

The solar-system kernel arc needs one question answered above all others: given a body and an instant, where is it? This crate answers it through a single trait, [`Ephemeris`], so that a second way of answering it — an analytic series with no data file, later — is a backend rather than a rewrite.

The backend that exists today reads a NAIF SPK kernel, the format JPL publishes the DE ephemerides in. It is implemented from NAIF's public format documents and checked against CSPICE over the same file; see [`spk`] for what that check requires and what the reader refuses to guess at.

A state is an ICRF position and velocity in kilometres and kilometres per second, relative to the solar-system barycentre — the ICRF origin is the barycentre by definition, so "barycentric" is not an extra convention here. The time argument is **TDB**, because that is what a kernel's epochs are; an epoch in any other scale is refused rather than converted silently, since the conversion is the caller's to make and `stkcraft-framework-time` can make it exactly.

No kernel is committed. `de440s.bsp` is 32 MB, it is fetched from NAIF with a pinned checksum when it is wanted (`AGENTS.md`: bulk data lives outside this repository), and the tests that need it say so when it is absent instead of passing as if they had run.

## stkcraft-agent-knowledge

The user's own documents, and the search that runs before a model answers.

`STKCraft` computes physics, and a plausible-looking number is worse than no number. A model asked "what is the maximum off-nadir angle for this sensor" will answer from its training data, which may be wrong, may be about another vehicle, and cannot be checked. **The person's own documents are the authority**, and this crate is how the platform reads them before the model speaks.

Point the library at a directory, and every readable document in it becomes searchable — text by line, a PDF by page:

- **Every answer can be traced to a place a person can open.** A hit names the document and the line range it came from, or the page and line range when the document is a PDF, so the interface can print the citation and a person can go and look.

- **Nothing is inferred.** Ranking is lexical (BM25 over words and CJK character pairs): the same library and the same query give the same order on every machine, which is what makes a regression test possible at all.

- **The model is told what it does not know.** When the search finds nothing above the threshold, [`Search::missed`] says so, and the agent's prompt requires the model to say that rather than invent a number.

- **Hostile input is bounded before it is read**: file count, file size, a directory depth and a skip list, so pointing the library at `/` is slow rather than fatal.

- **A re-open costs only what changed.** The derived index is cached in the key-value store, keyed by each file's path, size and modification time, so a paper corpus is parsed once and a second run is a directory walk.

- **A file that cannot be read is reported, not swallowed.** [`Opened::skipped`] names it and says why — a scan with no text layer, a PDF that will not open, a binary dressed as text — because a person who added a paper and cannot search it needs the reason.

No embeddings and no network. A vector index would need a model to build, which would make the retrieval non-deterministic and untestable, and the numbers this project cares about are *exact tokens* — a frequency, an angle, a file name — which lexical search matches better than a vector does. PDF and plain text are read; other binary formats (DOCX, XLSX, a scanned PDF with no text layer) are not, and the second of those is named in [`Opened::skipped`] rather than indexed as nothing. That is a stated limit, not a hidden one.

## stkcraft-framework-extensions

The extension package contract: what a theme, a plug-in or a skill pack may be.

`STKCraft` follows the `ArtCraft` family's extension model (`storytold/craft-extensions`), which is provisional upstream and deliberately narrow. This crate is the part of it that is pure data and validation: a package manifest, the rules an id and a path must satisfy, and the trust tier a package is assigned from *where it came from*. It reads no file it was not handed, unpacks no archive and touches no network — an unpacker is a separate, riskier thing.

[`TrustTier::ThirdParty`] exists, and [`Manifest::admit`] refuses it unless this crate was built with the `third-party` feature. No release build enables that feature, and the test below fails if it ever becomes a default, because opening the door is a decision the maintainers make after the gates in the family's threat model pass — not a side effect of a cargo dependency.

Nothing that matters. A manifest states its id, name, version, kind and what it targets; **it never states its own trust level**, because a package claiming to be trusted is exactly what an attacker would write. The host assigns the tier from where the package was found.

- **A theme carries no code**, so a theme manifest that names an entry point is refused.

- **A plug-in gets no capability in version 1**: no files, no network, no clock. Its permission list must be empty, and a manifest that asks for one is refused rather than silently ignored.

It is not the store, the installer, the unpacker or the signature check. Those are the family's `craft-ext-store` and they are not built here; until they are, a package on disk is data a person put there, and [`Manifest::parse`] is what decides whether it is well-formed.

## stkcraft-astro-engine

The `STKCraft` engine: the scenario, the commands, and the analysis that runs over them.

`STKCraft` is engine-first. Everything a user can do is a **command** with an id, a label, a menu path, parameter documentation, an `enabled` predicate and a `run` function. The menus, shortcuts, CLI, control channel and MCP server will all dispatch by id, which is what lets an agent do anything a user can — and it is why the engine comes before the viewport.

The layers below supply the physics:

- `stkcraft-framework-time` — epochs, scales and leap seconds.

- `stkcraft-astro-sgp4` — a two-line element set to a TEME state.

- `stkcraft-astro-frames` — TEME to GCRF and to Earth-fixed.

- `stkcraft-astro-access` — a station, a sensor and a position to access windows.

This crate holds them together: it owns the scenario document, moves each satellite from its element set through the frame chain to an Earth-fixed position, and hands that to the access layer.

There is no undo. The command table is exercised through the same dispatch path the window, CLI, control channel and MCP server use; those transports live in their own crates and reach the engine only through the registry.

## stkcraft-agent-mcp

The agent interface: `STKCraft` as an MCP server.

The engine's command registry is already the single door every transport goes through — a menu click, a keystroke, the CLI. This crate adds the last transport and the one that matters most for an agent-drivable tool: the Model Context Protocol, so a large language model can ask "what can you do?", run those commands, and read the methods and documents it needs.

A physics kernel that calls a language model would be a kernel that cannot be tested without a network, cannot be deterministic, and cannot answer why a number is what it is. So the model lives *outside*, on the other side of this protocol, and the kernel's job is to make itself completely usable from there: every command is a tool with a described schema, every skill is a prompt with the procedure it teaches, and the scenario is a resource an agent can read and write. The engine stays deterministic and the model stays replaceable — swapping GPT for a local model changes nothing in the kernel.

JSON-RPC 2.0 over standard input and output, one message per line, as the MCP specification for a stdio transport requires. [`Server::handle`] is the whole protocol and it is a pure function of a request and the session state, which is what makes it testable without a pipe: the transport loop in [`Server::serve`] only reads lines, hands them over and writes the answers.

## stkcraft-ui-viewport

The 3D viewport for `STKCraft`.

This crate draws; it does not compute. Everything it shows arrives in a [`Frame`] that the engine has already filled with positions, and the viewport's only job is to put them on the screen. That split is deliberate and is the reason replacing this crate cannot change an answer: an orbit drawn here is a polyline through propagated states, never a Keplerian ellipse reconstructed from elements.

This crate sits at the UI layer, above `LAST_NON_UI_LAYER` (defined in `xtask/src/layers.rs`), which is what allows it to depend on `wgpu` and `egui`. It depends on `stkcraft-framework-core` for units and errors and on nothing else from the engine, so the app can feed it from a live scenario, a saved file or a test fixture with no change here.

## stkcraft-agent-runtime

The model agent: a model driving the engine through its own tools.

This crate is the other half of the MCP server. `stkcraft-agent-mcp` lets a client *outside* the process — Claude Desktop, a local harness — drive the engine; this one lets the engine drive itself from a prompt, with the connection the person configured (`DeepSeek` is the default and [`ChatModel`] is a trait, so a different endpoint is a different provider rather than a second loop), and it is the same surface either way: the tools are the command registry's, executed through [`stkcraft_agent_mcp::Server`], and the skills are the same markdown documents.

1. The system prompt carries the mission, the tool discipline and the *names* of the skills.

2. The model answers with text, tool calls, or both.

3. Every tool call runs through the MCP server — the same JSON-RPC path a remote client uses, so an agent bug is a protocol bug and shows up in the MCP tests too.

4. Tool results go back as messages and the loop repeats, bounded by [`MAX_TURNS`].

5. The final text is the answer.

A system prompt that carried every skill would be long, expensive and mostly irrelevant to the question. The model is told which skills exist and calls [`SKILL_TOOL`] when it wants one — the same "progressive disclosure" an MCP client gets from `resources/list` and `prompts/get`.

The transport is `curl` on standard input, which is already how this repository fetches its bulk data: no TLS stack in the build, no HTTP client to audit, and the request and response are text a person can read when something goes wrong. [`ChatModel`] is a trait precisely so the tests never touch the network — a model that answers from a script exercises the whole loop.

## stkcraft-agent-control

The control channel: a local socket another program drives `STKCraft` through.

The Craft apps expose the same thing — `--control <port>`, a token file, JSON lines over loopback — so a launcher, a test harness or a sibling application can drive an app the way a person does: by running commands. This is that channel for `STKCraft`, and it is deliberately a *transport*, not a second implementation: every method here reaches the engine through the same command registry the menus, the CLI and the MCP server use.

A loopback port is not a permission: any process on the machine can connect to it. The token is written to a file only the user can read (`0600`, in `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR` when there is one), so "can drive this app" means "can read that file", which is the same set of processes that could edit the user's documents. The first request on a connection must be `auth`; everything else is refused until it is.

Not a way to run code: the methods are a fixed list, and the only one that changes anything is `engine.execute`, which runs a command from the registry — with the registry's own validation. A method that does not exist is an error naming the methods that do.
